rationale: The article is centrally about U.S. AI policy power brokers shaping restrictions on Chinese open-weight models and frontier AI oversight, making it highly relevant to AI policy despite limited broader pickup so far.

primary_article.title: A.I. Disproves a Decades-Old Mathematical Idea, the 'Biggest Conjecture' That the Tech Has Played a Role in Yet
primary_article.text:
A.I. Disproves a Decades-Old Mathematical Idea, the ‘Biggest Conjecture’ That the Tech Has Played a Role in Yet
A mathematician announced that he used one of Anthropic’s A.I. models to find a counterexample to a problem called the Jacobian conjecture. While experts consider it a milestone, the work raises questions about the future of mathematical research
While more than 60 million people in the United States watched the FIFA World Cup final on July 19, an artificial intelligence model was hard at work solving—or technically, disproving—a decades-old math problem.
Mathematician Levent Alpöge, of A.I. company Anthropic and Harvard University, used Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 to approach a mathematical conjecture: an idea that mathematicians believe to be true but has not yet been proven or disproven. He then posted an A.I.-assisted disproof on social media. It has since been verified by several independent mathematicians.
“hello there the jacobian conjecture is false,” Alpöge wrote on X. He thanked Akhil Mathew, a mathematician at the University of Chicago, for suggesting the problem and his “other close friend fable” for working during the match.
“This is a pretty big deal,” Abhishek Saha, a mathematician at Queen Mary University of London, tells New Scientist’s Matthew Sparkes. “Probably, this is the biggest conjecture that A.I. has played a significant role [in proving or disproving] so far in mathematics.”
hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx to my close friend akhil for asking about it and my other close friend fable for working during the world cup final
— levent (@__alpoge__) July 20, 2026
((1+xy)^3 z + y^2 (1+xy) (4+3xy), y + 3 x (1+xy)^2 z + 3 x y^2 (4+3xy), 2 x - 3 x^2 y - x^3 z): \C^3\to \C^3,…
In 1884, Czech mathematician Ludwig Kraus proposed a version of the Jacobian conjecture, which was expanded into its current form by German mathematician Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939.
The conjecture concerns polynomial functions, which behave like mathematical machines that take in one set of numbers and output a new set, writes Melissa Lee, a mathematician at Monash University in Australia, for the Conversation. Put in a set of numbers representing points in space—like coordinates on a map—and a function will move those numbers to new points according to the rules of the function.
“You can test how ‘nicely’ a function moves everything around in space by calculating something called the Jacobian determinant. If the Jacobian determinant is always a constant number that is not zero, then the function never folds or crushes space around a particular point,” Lee writes.
According to the conjecture, if the determinant is a nonzero constant, there should always be another function you can use to reverse all points to their original positions. Theoretically, it should be simple to disprove by finding a counterexample function that makes all the points merge and has a nonzero constant as the Jacobian determinant—but it’s proven far more challenging to do in real life. Mathematician Stephen Smale, a winner of the Fields Medal, often referred to as the Nobel Prize of mathematics, even included it on a 1998 list of 18 major mathematical problems for the 21st century.
Alpöge’s X post contains such a function. Using Fable, he found a three-dimensional function that has a constant Jacobian determinant and merges multiple input points, which makes it irreversible. This shows that the conjecture is false for spaces that are three or more dimensions, though it still could be true for lower-dimensional spaces.
Many outside researchers describe the result as a milestone for A.I.-assisted mathematics. Still, finding a single counterexample isn’t nearly as big a deal as proving the Jacobian conjecture, which hasn’t been done, Columbia University mathematician Andrew Blumberg tells Mashable’s Timothy Beck Werth. It mostly shows that there are “a lot of polynomials,” which are hard for humans alone to check.
A.I. could help prove conjectures, but at this point, the models aren’t able to provide reliable, step-by-step instructions for solving them, reports Fortune’s Eva Roytburg. Humans can fill more than 100 pages documenting just one proof.
Blumberg describes A.I.’s role with an analogy: “Suppose that Moses came down from the mountain with tablets, and on the tablet was written, ‘Cancer can be cured.’ Would you care? You don’t just want the answer to the question. You want to learn something from the answer,” he tells Mashable. “The reason Smale thought this problem was important is because he thought that if we solved it, we would understand more things about the about the way nature is structured.”
Nevertheless, the advance is widely seen as outpacing expectations for how soon A.I. would become useful in advanced mathematical research. In 2025, forefront models were able to solve five out of six problems at the International Mathematical Olympiad. And in May, OpenAI announced that a model from the company helped researchers solve an 80-year-old problem posed by Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdős. Following the announcement, OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck told the Wall Street Journal’s Ben Cohen that the prospect of that breakthrough would have seemed laughable even “a month ago.”
Quick fact: Mathematicians urge caution about A.I.
After that “Erdős problem” was solved with the help of A.I., 16 mathematicians published the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, which is endorsed by the International Mathematical Union. It calls on researchers to disclose their use of A.I., properly credit earlier work and publish their results in peer-reviewed outlets. It also warns against announcing claims before the mathematical community can evaluate them through formal channels.
Although the Jacobian counterexample is exciting, the shift toward A.I. in pure mathematics is “very rapid and very unsettling … especially for junior mathematicians,” says Mathew, who Alpöge mentioned in his X post, to Fortune.
It gets at the “how” without explaining the “why,” he adds. “One can check out that it’s correct, but it would be nice to be able to tell a story.”

rationale: The article is centrally about an AI-assisted mathematical breakthrough using Anthropic's model, potentially significant for AI-enabled research, but its direct relevance to a Stanford Law audience is moderate and the source is a credible popular-science secondary report with limited broader coverage.

primary_article.title: Can the New York Times Save Journalism From Our AI Overlords?
primary_article.text:
For most companies, spending upwards of $20 million on a single legal fight with an uncertain outcome might mean the boss has some explaining to do. For A.G. Sulzberger, the publisher of The New York Times, that explanation is simple: It’s the cost of defending journalism—at the Times and everywhere else.
Sulzberger, who took on the publisher role about a decade ago and has been an influential leader in the Times’ much-lauded push into digital innovation, has no shortage of defending to do lately. Nearly three years ago, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally used New York Times journalism to train AI models. That legal case, in which motions are still being filed about discovery requests, is only one front in a broader battle: The Trump administration is waging an ongoing war on press freedoms—most recently with an outrageous attempt to subpoena Times journalists over coverage of the president’s Qatar-gifted jet to be used as Air Force One—while AI companies radically reshape the way people find and consume information online.
The Times has arguably never been stronger as a business, having recently surpassed 13 million subscribers, and its newsroom is widely seen among journalists as one of the most stable and well-resourced in the business. Still, Sulzberger believes that journalism itself is facing myriad existential dilemmas—from an administration ready and willing to target reporters, from AI companies whose products depend on the very reporting they risk undermining, and media companies being demolished by the changes they’re unleashing on the open web.
I sat down with Sulzberger in late July at WIRED’s offices. We talked about that Times lawsuit, how and where AI is transforming reporting inside the newsroom, and why he thinks journalists and media executives need to team up—even while they continue to compete fiercely. You can read our entire conversation below, or listen to it here.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: AG, welcome. Thank you for being here.
A.G. SULZBERGER: It's great to be here. Thanks for inviting me.
I want to get into AI, and I will, but I would be a terrible journalist if I didn't start with news that has recently affected your paper.
Specifically, I'm talking about the subpoenas that the Justice Department has issued to several Times journalists about their reporting on the Air Force One jet that was gifted to the Trump administration by Qatar. The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to third-party phone service providers to obtain text messages and phone calls between some of those journalists and their family members.
Thanks for starting there, because it’s obviously yet another disturbing escalation in the Trump administration's efforts to punish and undermine the free press in this country.
First I should say, I have so much admiration for the reporters who have done this work and who are doing it under a different kind of pressure than we have seen in generations. I think that by any objective metric, this is the biggest effort to go after the press that we've seen from a White House probably since Woodrow Wilson, so in more than a century.
These reporters just continued, day after day, to put their heads down, right? Not to get baited by the folks booing them or the folks cheering them on, and just to do their work. That work includes reporting things that the President of the United States doesn't want the public to know because it may be unflattering or embarrassing.
In this case, they reported a story, as you said, on the Qatari-donated jet, and it's a little unclear: Was it donated to the Trump administration or to Trump himself? A donation worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Right.
When that occurred, a lot of people had questions about whether it could ever be secure enough to hold the President of the United States and ferry him around the world. Sure enough, our reporters found out that on one of its inaugural trips, its first trip overseas to Turkey, there were concerns that it was insufficiently equipped to respond to a threat, that the president had to fly back on the original Air Force One. He denied this initially. But we exposed the truth, which has subsequently been confirmed.
Then it gets even stranger.
Every administration, we will publish something that the President of the United States doesn't want the American people to know. Upsetting a president of either party is nothing new to us. What is new is that the administration defied many of its own standards and practices and explicit guidelines to very rapidly, in the course of a day or two, serve subpoenas on these reporters. They went straight to the homes of reporters, in an obvious attempt to intimidate them. As you said, we are now learning that they sought to get records, not just from the reporters themselves, but from members of their families. It's a gross overreach.
Just to contextualize for listeners, how unusual is all of that? To have law enforcement at your home as a journalist, to be subpoenaed right out of the gate, to have those phone records called up by the Justice Department. How weird is that?
I mean, it's extremely unusual. It's very rare. The closest comparison that I have had at the Times in my tenure—I've been in this job roughly a decade—happened in the first Trump administration, when some of our reporter records were secretly seized by the Justice Department. In fact, that led to some reforms in the Justice Department aimed at curtailing that type of abuse.
On one side this is objectively very rare—there was similar overreach, you may remember, in a Washington Post case some months ago, where they actually raided the reporter's home and seized her devices—[but] on the other [hand], this is building naturally off of what I think is a broader effort.
You have also criticized other media outlets for capitulating to the administration, particularly around settling what you've called winnable cases to appease Trump. Do you still see your peers as largely capitulating?
I don't think I ever said largely capitulating. I actually think that the industry has largely held its ground. And to be very clear, holding your ground does not mean an adversarial posture. It means being willing to publish the truth even when powerful people get angry at you for publishing it.
It means being willing to ask any question, no matter who it might upset. I actually think that the industry, by and large, has done very good work. WIRED’s done good work. The [Wall Street] Journal has done terrific work. The Associated Press. When the White House conditioned their continued access to the White House on them switching from calling a big body of water the Gulf of America instead of the Gulf of Mexico, they didn’t take that sitting down.
I remember this.
They sued, and I think rightly. They sued regardless of whether they win the case, right?
Right.
One of the things that I'm saying to peers in the industry regularly is that your rights only hold if you seek to enforce them.
You may not win every battle, but the surest way to lose your rights is to avert your eyes, drop your head, and try to avoid notice and just take what comes.
I do think that some news organizations have clearly felt the pressure from the administration and I think allowed that pressure to affect coverage.
My colleagues in Washington tell me that they're regularly talking to reporters at other news organizations who are saying that they will no longer pursue certain stories, because they're too worried that their editors will kill them because of fear of retaliation, and that their model is actually to wait for an institution like the Times to report the story, and then they'll follow it, and they think that that's a fight they can win. But breaking the story, being the one to first upset the White House, seems like a road too far.
That is the definition of chilling, right? That's when the message that retaliation and punishment must be avoided gets down to the lowest levels of the newsroom. Now, my job as publisher of the Times is to make sure the opposite message is getting through, right?
After these great reporters were served these subpoenas, I called each of them and I said, “We have your back, and we'll do whatever we need to support you.” One of the things that I was most encouraged to hear in those conversations, although not surprised, these are tough guys, was that they said, “Oh, we're not gonna let go of this story.”
Good. As a journalist myself, and I run a publication that takes heat here and there, I worry sometimes about how we better translate that to the audience. So making sure the public understands how essential this work is, and exposing them to the work itself, especially in the context of AI. How do you think about that? What else can news organizations be doing to make sure that audiences are exposed to the work and see and understand the value of the work, and what it means when that work stops happening?
Look, I agree that we haven't done good enough of a job as an industry on that. We've sort of taken it for granted. At the Times I think about just the outsize investment we are making on behalf of the public's right to know. We put reporters on the ground in 150 countries last year. Every year, over 150 countries. Last year, we had reporters on the ground in Myanmar, in Sudan, in Lebanon, in Iran, in Venezuela, in Gaza, in Israel, in Russia.
In Ukraine alone, we had more than 70 journalists on the ground. And I am sure, although we've never done it, that if we dug in, it's really hard to find the financial case for those expenditures.
Yes. I would agree with you there.
I am sure, though I've never done it, that when I look at all the investigative reporting we've done, and this is reporting that takes months, sometimes years of work to produce a single story, that it would be very hard to justify all those expenditures, right?
But I think the public sometimes doesn't know how much institutions like ours think about the civic good. I really believe, as our Founding Fathers did, and across all their lines of division, the Founding Fathers agreed that a free people need a free press and that a country that aimed to steer itself needed access to independent and reliable information.
Jefferson famously said, given the choice between a government without a press or a press without the government, he wouldn't hesitate to choose the press. And that's because this work really does matter to society.
Journalism is quite simply very often how you know what you know. Shifting over to AI, it's how AI knows what it knows.
Yes, let's get into that. In the context of AI in journalism, I break it into two buckets. For WIRED, there's reporting on this technological moment in time, which is really important. And then there's the separate question, although we cover that as well, of how AI will affect the practice of journalism and the consumption of journalism.
I mean, there are really difficult lines to walk here, and I'm curious about how you think about that at The Times.
I think my philosophy is you very rarely in life need to be first. There is a risk of jumping too quickly into an emerging technology. And there's probably more risk in that than waiting, watching, learning, studying, experimenting quietly behind the scenes. I think you saw some of those risks, right? Like, think about the news organizations that, in my mind incredibly foolishly, decided to just hand over full responsibility for writing and publishing articles to AI. Mistakes were made.
Mistakes were made. And mistakes were published.
That is right. And not just mistakes were published, but fake journalists were invented. It was a completely foreseeable and unnecessary set of mistakes. Humans are responsible for everything we produce, period. And there's something about AI that has tricked people into forgetting that it is a tool.
Well, it's a very good conversation partner.
But when my colleagues say, "Well, what if AI makes a mistake?" I say, "Well, then it’s your job to find that mistake and take it out of your work." You would never ask that about a computer. What if a computer makes a mistake?
Well, you gotta find it, right? I view this as a reporting tool. So we're using it much more in reporting than writing, crafting, editing.
I think AI is very good at spotting patterns and anomalies in large data sets. In many ways, that's a pretty good summation of a big part of reporting. You know, campaign finance reporting is basically what are the patterns, how is the mix of donors to the Republicans and Democrats changing, big donors for small donors, and then anomalies.
One of the reporters who won our first Pulitzer that involved AI-supported reporting, what he said to me is, "You have to think of AI as a filter.”
In his case, he was examining bomb craters in the Israel-Gaza conflict, and he said that it regularly makes a certain kind of mistake. So the way to think about AI is it took millions of images and it shrunk it down to thousands of images. But it was his job as a journalist to look at every one of those thousands of images to make sure he felt confident in the findings.
So that's the type of experiment we're doing, and I think between that natural posture of, we wanna take our time and move with curiosity and creativity, but also some degree of care and caution, and that we as journalists, as reporters, as editors, are ultimately responsible for the work.
I think that's how we've avoided most mistakes.
I agree with you. I think it is a very valuable tool, or can be used to create very valuable tools, for reporting and for reporters, especially as newsrooms have gotten smaller. I think there's a competitive advantage there. I will say at WIRED we are building our own AI tools for reporting, and one of the goals is actually to beat The New York Times more often. So we're trying to get clever in ways that maybe other news organizations aren't when it comes to using AI.
Everyone needs competition. So we'll watch with interest.
But in a speech recently, you also said there are early signs to be concerned about when it comes to how AI will affect fact-based reporting. I mean, some of those are obvious. But talk to me about what you see as those early signs. What worries you most here?
It's really important just to go back to what I referred to in that speech as the original sin of AI.
There are four ingredients in good AI products: There are the people who write the code; there is what we call compute, the chips and data centers, et cetera; there is electricity; and there is what Silicon Valley calls data but which is content, journalism, books, music, movies.
And let's just go through those four right now. On the coders, you literally have contracts that are sports-star level.
Oh, they're paid like NBA players. It's outrageous.
Hundreds of millions of dollars for a single individual coder at times. Now let's look at compute and electricity. Literally, these companies are taking hundreds of billions of dollars of debt in order to pay for those things. That's how big the prize is if they win. These are companies that all now have trillion-dollar valuations or near-trillion-dollar valuations, right? So the prize is big.
Now you get to data, and they've just taken it. They've just taken it all. Without permission and without any compensation, because they thought they could. They think they can get away with it. And if they can get away with that, then that boosts the profit margins of the richest and most valuable companies in the history of humanity. And if the casualty is that it completely guts what remains of our already financially beleaguered industry of journalism, so be it.
If it completely undermines the financial models for professions like book writing and music making and movies and TV and academic research, then so be it.
That is objectively the wrong thing to do. It is also not allowed under US law. Protections for what is called intellectual property date back all the way to the Constitution, so it is not legal to come in and take all this work.
Why does this all matter? Why do I feel some degree of alarm about this? You know it has already been challenging to compete with the giant platforms that basically exercise a monopoly over human attention, right?
That's a little overstated, but if you added up all the minutes of a day, a handful of platforms and a handful of companies occupy the vast majority of those, right? But now you're not just competing with companies that are controlling the vast majority of human attention, right? Companies that are actually designed to be maximally intermediating. Companies that feel that AI will work best if it sits in between the user and the content creator.
Google is one sort of really salient example here.
It's hard to overstate the degree to which publishers relied on traffic from Google referral links and the degree to which that traffic has disappeared in the last year, year-and-a-half, as Google has introduced AI. So now when you search, you get an AI Overview.
It's reasonably helpful, usually helpful enough that you don't need to click through. Even just that change has been crushing.
And you are suing, you are in a years-long lawsuit. You said recently you've spent, what, $20 million on this legal battle against several big AI companies for copyright infringement. How is that suit going, if I may ask?
And I'm curious, what is your ideal outcome from that lawsuit, not just for The New York Times but for the news industry more broadly. What do you hope to accomplish there?
Let me first just linger on the number you just said. We are two and a half years into this lawsuit. Two and a half years. And we have spent well over $20 million on this lawsuit, and we are not yet through discovery.
I didn't realize that. Wow.
Yeah. So when you think about this original sin, this theft of every creative work ever created, it amounts to this immense wealth transfer, right? From creators and researchers around the world to the biggest tech companies in the history of humanity. That sense of impunity that they can just take our stuff is happening in part because of how expensive it is to enforce your rights. The Times, thankfully, we've worked really hard to put ourselves in a financial position where we can enforce our rights.
Can you imagine being a small-town newspaper and being able to take on Google or OpenAI or Microsoft or Perplexity.
I mean, it's not gonna happen.
It's impossible. It's just completely unfeasible. So these companies have been backed into this awful position, where AI companies have already stolen your stuff. They say explicitly they're going to use it regardless, and then sometimes they'll throw a little bit of money your way. What do you do? Do you try to spend what may end up being $40 million on a lawsuit? Or do you accept the pennies on every dollar you spent to create your work just to recoup something?
We think it's really important to enforce our rights and say “absolutely not.” Like, you want to use our stuff, that requires permission, and that requires fair compensation.
Someone needs to fight that fight. Thankfully, we're not the only ones filing a lawsuit like this. A number of other publishers in the industry have filed similar lawsuits.
Our parent company has a few.
Silicon Valley has tried to portray our lawsuit as anti-tech.
They have.
It is not anti-tech. It is anti-theft, and anytime you hear the anti-tech line, I just want you to picture Jensen Huang coming down onto the floor of his Nvidia factory, discovering that Sam Altman has snuck in and has arms full of chips and he's running out of the building.
What a visual.
And Jensen says, "Hey, you're not allowed to take that." And Sam Altman says, "If you tell me that I can't take this, you're anti-tech, Jensen. You're gonna make China win."
We are not anti-tech. We are anti-theft. This is not about money. This is about the ability to sustain essential work.
You've talked a few times about our profession, journalists and news executives, linking hands on this issue of AI. Teaming up to get ahead of it, to win. What does it look like to you to compete and team up at the same time? Because we all compete fiercely.
Well, who would you say was the closest, fiercest competitor of The New York Times if you look at the last half century? The Washington Post.
I was thinking it in my head, trying to be emotionally generous. But that is the answer.
The Washington Post was our fiercest competitor. And boy are they fierce.
And to their credit, they still are.
To this day, there are so many good journalists at The Washington Post, and not a week goes by without them publishing something that I'm just salivating with envy over them having gotten first. So they were our fiercest competitors. They were also our closest ally when our industry came under pressure.
Just think about the Pentagon Papers. The New York Times starts publishing the Pentagon Papers. The Nixon White House goes to war with The Times. It is so dark. The threats are intensifying so much that my grandfather, who was publisher at the time, has his entire legal team quit over his decision to publish the stories, and they tell him he may spend the rest of his life in jail.
And he starts carrying a toothbrush in his pocket, in case he's hauled off at any moment.
The fresh breath was really important?
Fresh breath was really important to him in prison. So we publish the stories, we defy the Nixon White House, and eventually we will win the legal case that establishes the right that the government cannot establish what's called prior restraint, keep you from publishing something in advance.
We will end up winning that legal right. But there's a period in which we are locked down. When the court has ordered us to halt publication. And what happens the next day? The Washington Post picks up where we left off. And I could give you a dozen of those stories.
Our journalists were all kicked out of China in retaliation for some of the actions of the first Trump administration. Who was my first call? It was Fred Ryan at The Washington Post. And my second call was Will Lewis at The Wall Street Journal, and we decided that we would raise concerns about these actions collectively.
Let's compete on the stories all day long. Let's compete for the best journalists all day long. And then when our rights are attacked—the same rights that protect me are the rights that protect you and vice versa—we all come together. I think that's the posture we need in the face of these AI abuses.
There are things we can do collectively. We can tell the story of these abuses and help the public understand them. We can tell the story of journalism, what journalism is and why it matters, and the danger it faces if these abuses are allowed to continue. We can enforce our rights.
How do you win? How does our industry win? Our industry is not gonna win compared to the tech giants. We are a tiny little minnow.
Well, let’s say winning is synonymous with surviving.
And that's it. What I am worried about, and what you're worried about, and all our peers across the industry, is not about getting giant and bigger. That's what the folks in Silicon Valley are worried about. They want to take over the world. We want an essential profession, an essential service. The act of seeking the truth, helping people understand the world, holding power to account. We want that to survive, and I really believe that democracy needs it to survive.
Who else does these things if journalists don't? Is AI going to go to the front lines of the Ukraine conflict and show what's happening there? Is AI going to spend years building the sources that we need to finally get Trump's taxes and provide the fullest picture of Trump's wealth and the conflicts inherent in that.
AI can't do any of those things. And so we need journalists for it, and AI needs journalists for it. So we need to come up with a sustainable framework for all of this.
And I would argue one that ensures that The New York Times is not the only game in town. You guys need competitors.
Look, we are the first to say that.
I mean, you are a behemoth.
It's interesting that you say that we're a behemoth, and you cover behemoths here at WIRED.
You are a behemoth in the context of the news industry.
I really want to slow it down. The newsroom at The New York Times, we're really proud of it, has basically doubled the number of journalists that we have to 2,400. That is a drop in the bucket of the number of journalists that this country needs.
I could not agree more.
We’ve reached this amazing milestone. We hit 13 million subscribers. We're aiming for 15, and that sounds like a big number until you remember that Netflix is over 300 million, and you have another, you know, half dozen with a hundred, 200 million subscribers.
Actually it's all the way down the list to Crunchyroll. Crunchyroll has more subscribers than The New York Times. We are the largest player in our beleaguered industry. But what we need is the entire industry to be much bigger. If you're going to say that The New York Times is the country's leading news organization, do we really think that the country's leading news organization should have fewer subscribers than an anime streaming service?
Well, when you put it like that, A.G., I agree. What I want is for a 23-year-old journalist to look at this industry and think, "I could work there, I could work there, I could work there. Or maybe I could work there." There are not enough places to point to.
I mean, there are other success stories. I think The Journal has been doing extraordinarily well and doing great work. The Post had an amazing decade and before a couple of really tough years. The Atlantic, The New Yorker. Bloomberg may still be the largest newsroom in America.
But there aren't enough. And particularly at the local level. We've seen an 80 percent loss in the number of working journalists at the local level in this country over the last two decades.
It is completely untenable, and it is not good for anyone. One of the things that makes me appreciate Meredith [Kopit Levien] so much, she's our CEO, she's the top commercial leader of the organization, and any time she is asked, she says, “I would much rather build a market for journalism than to build a business for journalism,” like a private business.
She wants to build up that market, because the more we build up that market, the stronger we will all be. You'll have more talent in the market. You will have more competition for stories, which makes us all stronger.
It's also just really important for America. Studies show that when you lose local journalism in your community, basically every unhealthy civic metric goes up. Loneliness goes up, distrust goes up, voting goes down. Corruption goes up.
When you've got a strong local news organization, I think about Minneapolis, the Star Tribune, or The Seattle Times, the Baltimore Banner is doing amazing work. You see better civic outcomes. So I think it's important for the industry; it's important for the country.
Let me end on this, because we've talked about a bunch of really tough stuff. Crunchyroll will stay with me. What makes you optimistic? When you wake up in the morning or you're going to bed at night and you have a million things to worry about, you have a two-and-a-half-year, $20-million-plus lawsuit among them, you have the Justice Department knocking on the door of your journalists, what gives you hope and optimism for this industry?
It's a good question. This feels like a moment of great challenge, of existential challenge for our profession.
I try not to force myself to avert my eyes from that. Because you want to avert your eyes from that. But I think the AI challenge, I think the press freedom challenge, I think also the challenge of serving this incredibly polarized, tribalized public—I think of those as sort of the three great challenges of my tenure, and those are first and foremost.
At the end of the hardest days, what makes me feel like it's all worth it—and this isn't to sound corny, it's true, and you can ask my kids, because they're always complaining about it—is reading the paper. Just to remind myself, “Oh, this is what I'm fighting for.”

primary_article.title: Off-grid data centers aren't the panacea that some AI firms hoped
primary_article.text: Local backlash and reliability concerns are challenging the vision of an AI boom built quickly using large off-grid data centers. Why it matters: If giant projects stumble, trillions of dollars in AI investment and the industry's plans to rapidly expand data centers could be at risk. The big picture: In an effort to speed AI development, some companies are building data centers powered mainly by onsite generation rather than waiting years to connect to the electric grid. There are 59 data centers with a combined capacity of about 90 gigawatts that plan to build their own power "behind-the-meter" using sources like gas turbines, generators and fuel cells, according to a report from research firm Cleanview. A smaller subset is trying to run large campuses mostly on behind-the-meter power as a way to move more quickly than the local utility and the grid can. Infrastructure risk analysis firm Occam Edge tracks 12 projects where on-site power is the primary serving supply, representing about 10.6 GW of announced capacity. State of play: Recent hiccups are highlighting the challenges that come with bypassing the grid. Earlier this month, New Mexico's top land official rejected a gas pipeline meant to supply on-site fuel cells for Oracle's 2.5 GW Project Jupiter data center campus, part of Oracle and OpenAI's Stargate initiative. The regulatory setback could contribute to a yearslong delay . A week later, a much smaller off-grid data center in Virginia , saw its on-site gas turbines knocked offline for 24 hours , forcing it to run on dirty backup diesel generators during already bad air quality from the Canadian wildfires. Local residents complained of burning lungs and 60-decibel noise, and a local government official called for new laws to regulate generators. Catch up quick: Chief developers of this off-grid approach include OpenAI, and its partners Oracle and Crusoe, which have worked on OpenAI's Stargate campuses. A Stargate project in Abilene, Texas, developed by Crusoe, reportedly went offline for days at a time due to issues with power and cooling equipment. Another off-grid player is Elon Musk, who rattled the energy world when he built xAI's Colossus 1 using mobile gas turbines in just a few months. While it was initially off-grid, it's now grid-connected and selling compute to Anthropic. Despite a lawsuit from the NAACP over Colossus 1, Musk is now using gas turbines to power Colossus 2 (with compute sold to Google), and earlier this month bought a mobile gas turbine company. What they're saying: Critics argue off-grid data centers could prove slower and more costly to deploy, less reliable to run, and more expensive than expanding the electric grid. "This is a flimsy way to deploy AI," says energy investor Jigar Shah, who predicts much of the bullish off-grid deployment figures won't materialize. Power engineers are worried that off-grid data centers won't meet reliability targets, says Occam Edge founder and CEO Christian Okoye, who compares "Dark Gigawatts" to the "Dark Fiber" of the dotcom bust. "It's a time of desperation," says Josh Wong, founder and CEO of ThinkLabs AI, which helps utilities find more capacity on their current grids. "The [off-grid] business model is bolt-on." Follow the money: Investors are lacking insight into the reliability of off-grid data centers, says Okoye. Investors faced with the uncertainties of off-grid data centers could decide not to underwrite them. S&P Global Ratings recently downgraded Oracle's long-term issuer credit rating to BBB- from BBB, just one step above junk status, due to its massive data center spending, which includes investment in on-site power infrastructure. Trillions of dollars are riding on whether large off-grid data centers can work as advertised, justify their added cost and win local support. What's next: More high-profile problems building and running off-grid data centers could lead to a reckoning that the AI boom will be a lot more grid-powered than many AI companies hoped.

rationale: The article is centrally about AI data center expansion and off-grid power challenges, with significant implications for AI infrastructure, energy policy, local regulation, and sustainability, though it is less directly tied to legal AI or higher education.

primary_article.title: Unionized workers are bargaining with the bots
primary_article.text: With Congress on the sidelines, union contracts are among the strongest guardrails American workers have against artificial intelligence . Why it matters: Nearly 90% of the U.S. workforce lacks union representation, leaving about 130 million workers without that leverage as companies use AI to rewrite job descriptions and cut jobs. What they're saying: The only meaningful guardrails around workplace AI are happening "at the bargaining table , where workers are showing up and demanding protections," NewsGuild-CWA President Jon Schleuss tells Axios. "AI is something we can negotiate," Schleuss says. "Without a contract and without a union , you have no say." Former FTC Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya notes that union-negotiated rules could easily map onto federal policy — if Congress ever finds the political will. Case in point: The NewsGuild currently has between 85 and 90 contracts with explicit AI provisions, Schleuss says. At Politico, unionized reporters forced management into arbitration after the newsroom introduced inaccurate AI reporting tools without the union's permission. Management dismantled the tools. Entertainment union SAG-AFTRA negotiated workplace protections that prohibit AI replicas replacing actors without the actors's consent. A union representing workers at ZeniMax, the Microsoft-owned video game company, won contract provisions requiring AI to support — not replace — workers. The agreement also requires management to notify the union and negotiate before deploying new AI tools. The big picture: AI protections are gaining ground fastest in industries with longer histories of unionization and repeated threats to workers' livelihoods, including manufacturing, journalism and entertainment. White collar workers like those in Big Tech with high wages and corporate perks had something of an "illusion of protection" that made them avoid organized labor, TechEquity's Tim Newman says. Now, companies are using AI as a pretext for layoffs to appease Wall Street, shattering that illusion. Sean Fern, a principal infrastructure engineer at NAVA PBC and a member of its bargaining committee, notes a "large groundswell" of tech workers organizing after realizing "even a good performing engineer can sometimes lose their job overnight, given no fault of their own, and they don't see themselves as quite so special anymore." Between the lines: Existing labor statutes like the 1988 WARN Act were built for 20th-century mass factory closures — not remote tech workers, gig economy contractors or quiet algorithmic layoffs. By the numbers: About 16.5 million U.S. workers were represented by unions in 2025, the highest number in 16 years, according to an Economic Policy Institute analysis of federal data . That amounts to just 11.2% of workers, but the rate varies drastically by industry and job. About 36% of education, training, and library employees are unionized . Just 4.4% of workers in computer occupations are represented by unions. In finance, it's a mere 1.1%. Zoom out: Some states have begun to regulate AI's role in the workplace. But Congress has made little progress. Too many elected officials are "taking a lot of credit for holding a roundtable, and that is not where we should be right now," says Bedoya. Federal progress amounts to "baby steps," says Lauren McFerran, a former National Labor Relations Board chair who now leads the AFL-CIO Tech Institute. She blames massive lobbying budgets: "It's kind of a classic people versus money issue." The Tech Institute backs several bills, she says, including the No Robot Bosses Act , the Stop Spying Bosses Act , the No Fakes Act and the AI Civil Rights Act . The bottom line: America is quickly becoming a patchwork of protections. Those with a union contract have a say in their technological future. Those who don't may be on their own. rationale: The article is centrally about workplace AI protections through union bargaining, with meaningful labor and policy implications for legal audiences, though it is more of a trend analysis than a major new AI development and appears to have limited broader pickup.

primary_article.title: AI’s finally expensive enough to make Wall Street nervous
primary_article.text:
It’s earnings season, and investors got an unpleasant surprise from Google: an increase on its spending estimate, to as much as $205 billion — from the last quarter’s projection of up to $190 billion. Even the lower end of Google’s new projected range — $195 billion — is much more than the company had previously forecast as its top end spending. Now, look, I recognize that there’s an impulse to say things like “What’s $15 billion between friends?” but from an investor’s perspective, Google has essentially said that it can’t accurately forecast its costs, which is a scary thing. Plus, Google is spending more money than it’s making. And Google is also facing competitive pressures from Chinese AI tools, as well as pricing pressure to keep the cost of its models low.
AI’s finally expensive enough to make Wall Street nervous
The joys of quarterly earnings!
The joys of quarterly earnings!
You don’t have to be a finance genius to figure out that spending more than you make isn’t an ideal business practice. What’s more, increased spending in an environment where you have to either keep your prices static or drop them doesn’t bode well. You’re spending more and getting the same amount back, or — worse — spending more for less revenue.
“A reminder of funding strain in the AI build-out.”
These pressures aren’t just on Google. They’re on the entire AI ecosystem. Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft will all report their earnings this week, and there are plenty of people who think they will also announce they are spending more than expected on the data center buildout.
There are a few other things happening at the same time that suggest investors are getting nervous. First of all, people seem to have finally noticed that SpaceX sucks; as of this writing, its shares are worth almost half as much as they were during its peak. Second, investors are nervous about Oracle’s datacenter buildout debt, and it’s worth keeping in mind that Oracle is the public market’s stand-in for OpenAI. Third, Nvidia has been engaging in rounds of deal talks worth a combined three-quarters of a trillion dollars. Nvidia — even more so than OpenAI — is at the center of the circular financing in the AI ecosystem. If it is pumping more money into supporting the AI buildout, that may be an indication that the actual demand is weaker than expected.
Specifically, Nvidia guaranteeing OpenAI’s debt, a deal worth $250 billion, is “as much a reminder of funding strain in the AI build-out as it is a demand signal,” Billy Leung, Global X Management’s tech sector investment strategist, told Bloomberg.
On top of all that, a Chinese start-up released a new model, and people get nervous every time that happens. One reason for that nervousness is that China’s biggest constraint is that they — at least theoretically — don’t have the same kind of access to GPUs as US companies, and yet their AI systems are still competitive. If that is indeed what is happening, there’s an end in sight to Nvidia (and other chipmakers’) cash bonanza. What’s more, it may mean that companies are building too many data centers.
I’ve spoken to a lot of smart people who are more optimistic than I am about the AI boom. (I have been asking how AI companies plan to actually make money for three years now, and I still have not received a satisfactory answer.) All of them think we will likely overbuild data centers during this period of exuberance. They also think that a lot of AI companies will die off when the inevitable correction comes. They are invested in the space anyway because they think the companies that survive will make them more money than they will lose on the ones that die off.
So the AI boosters are watching for the market top just like everyone else; they know it’s inevitable. It’s hard to figure out what the market top is in advance, of course. But some investors are clearly starting to get cold feet about the whole AI thing, and they’re moving their money elsewhere.
We may very well get earnings from the other big tech companies that reassure investors, and this period of AI anxiety will pass. On the other hand, if you’re looking for top signals, Elon Musk is a pretty good one, and SpaceX did just go public. Best of luck to all of us, I guess!

rationale: The article is centrally about rising AI infrastructure costs and investor concern around major AI companies, but it is mainly market analysis rather than a new legal, policy, or technical development.

primary_article.title: Anthropic, OpenAI blow past Starbucks, McDonald's amid AI boom
primary_article.text: Data: Company reports, Funda via "Key Context"; Chart: Ben Berkowitz/Axios AI revenue is accelerating so fast that it's starting to dwarf some of the world's most recognizable brands. Why it matters: AI infrastructure spending forecasts in the trillions of dollars start to make at least a little more sense when investors see how they're paying off. By the numbers: OpenAI and Anthropic, combined, are on track for an annual revenue rate of about $120 billion, "Key Context" Substack author Tae Kim noted on Monday, via data from AI investment research platform Funda . Anthropic makes up about 60% of that, given the company's lead with corporate customers (a lead that OpenAI is working to shrink). Both would land in the Fortune 500's top 100 companies by revenue at those levels. Stunning stat: At around $71 billion in estimated annual revenue, Anthropic would best Starbucks ($37.2 billion) and McDonald's ($26.9 billion) combined. It would almost top both of them plus Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands as well. Those international brands are 50 to 100 years old, with tens of thousands of locations and nearly universal recognition; Anthropic was just founded five years ago. The bottom line: Who needs to eat out when Claude can just give you the recipe.

rationale: The article is squarely about AI company revenue growth and the broader AI boom, but it is a short business-data comparison rather than a major new announcement or legal/policy development of special relevance to the Stanford Law audience.

primary_article.title: A million words costs $50 from Anthropic and 87 cents from DeepSeek. Corporate America noticed.
primary_article.text:
Roughly 750,000 words of AI output costs $50 if you buy it from Anthropic’s Fable. The same volume from DeepSeek’s V4-Pro costs about 87 cents, Fortune reported. Z.AI’s GLM-5.2 charges $4.40. Moonshot’s Kimi K3, pricey by Chinese standards, charges $15.
Corporate America has noticed. Companies spent a year competing to burn tokens. Now they shop for the cheapest model that can finish the job, the Wall Street Journal reported. The badge of honour used to be tokenmaxxing. The new one is thrift-maxxing.
The first response to the bills was rationing, when firms capped what staff could spend. The second is substitution, and it is a far bigger problem for OpenAI and Anthropic.
“It’s like driving a Lamborghini to go to the grocery store to pick up milk when that was designed to be raced around a track,” said Mike Saeks, a field chief technology officer at Cursor who advises companies on their AI returns.
He has the receipts. Cursor priced up building a web browser from scratch. Running the whole job on OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 cost a little over $10,000. Splitting it between Cursor’s own Composer model and Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 cost $1,339.
The orchestra, not the soloist
This is not companies abandoning American labs. It is companies demoting them to the parts of the job that justify the price.
Telnyx, which builds infrastructure for AI agents, ran 1,000 of them on a top Anthropic model under a $200-per-employee subscription. Then Anthropic stopped allowing third-party operating systems on subscriptions, treating it as a breach of its terms. Paying per use instead would have cost “like 100 grand per day”, chief executive David Casem told the Journal.
So Telnyx rebuilt the stack. Z.AI models now run its 1,400 agents. Anthropic’s Fable acts as the conductor and plans the work. Open-weight models handle the implementation. OpenAI’s Sol reviews what they produce.
The legal AI startup Harvey trained GLM-5.2 itself. It then gave the model a button to call Fable 5 when a task looks genuinely hard. “We work with all of them,” said president Gabe Pereyra. Zoom’s chief technology officer Xuedong Huang reached for an old Chinese story. In it, three ordinary people combine their wits to match one genius. That, he said, is the secret sauce.
“It really feels like a bloodbath”
The labs are reacting the way any supplier does when switching costs collapse. They are paying customers to stay.
“There’s zero loyalty that I’m seeing,” said Marty Kausas, chief executive of the customer support platform Pylon. “It really feels like a bloodbath right now.” Pylon has been handed months of unlimited free usage. Kausas reckons it has taken about $1.6m in free tokens from one vendor this year. Another gave $65,000, and a third gave $10,000.
Both labs say they are adapting. An OpenAI spokeswoman said GPT-5.6 Sol was trained to be far more token efficient. Anthropic released a powerful lower-cost model on Friday. An executive said customers can choose intelligence or price inside its own ecosystem. Both say they support open-weight models.
Why the gap is so wide
The price difference is not charity. Electricity costs less in China, and new data centres there meet less local resistance. Chinese firms are also willing to run thin margins to win share and become the default.
Export controls may have helped. Cut off from the best Nvidia chips, Chinese labs had to squeeze more out of worse hardware. “For the money [a Chinese AI company would] spend on an Nvidia chip, they can buy 10 local chips from Huawei or other local chipmakers,” George Chen of the Asia Group told Fortune.
From Coinbase to DoorDash
Household names are doing it too. Coinbase chief executive Brian Armstrong said in June that the exchange had halved its AI spending. It did so by pushing staff towards Kimi and Z.AI’s GLM models.
DoorDash sends what its chief technology officer Andy Fang calls “lower-level work” to Kimi, for “better quality [at] cheaper cost”. Airbnb has used Alibaba’s Qwen for customer service. Cursor built its own Composer 2 coding model on Kimi foundations.
The result shows up in usage. Chinese models took 57% of the tokens US firms consumed on OpenRouter during one week in July. At one point mid-month, all five of the marketplace’s top models were Chinese.
It reaches well beyond developers. IDC surveyed 260 decision-makers at US firms with more than 1,000 staff. Of those, 47% said they used a made-in-China model for at least one use case, The Daily Upside reported. One in five reported extensive use.
The IPO problem
Here is why this lands harder than an ordinary price war. OpenAI and Anthropic spent years racing to build the most capable models. Then they found that plenty of customers want basic ones. Both are preparing to list publicly. The Journal reports the shift is threatening the valuations they carry into those listings.
It also explains the lobbying. The fight over restricting Chinese open-weight models has run all month. It stretches from the startups opposing a ban to the giants who signed a letter defending open models on Friday. The price sheet is what that argument is actually about.
The market has already voted once. Moonshot announced K3 on 16 July. Nvidia lost almost $600bn in value and briefly ceded its place as the world’s most valuable company to Apple.
Reasons to keep your head
Not everyone thinks the sky is falling. On TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane argued the industry does this every time. “We’re now a week out and I don’t think anybody’s feeling like the end is nigh like they were a week ago,” he said.
His colleague Kirsten Korosec asked the sharper question about a ban. “Are we accelerating and ensuring that Americans win the AI race, or are we ensuring that certain frontier labs do better than others?”
Real frictions remain. Gartner’s Igor Marchal warned about going public with it. Naming a Chinese model invites suspicion at best, he wrote, and reputational damage and procurement pushback at worst. Congress is probing Airbnb and Cursor over their use of such models.
The big clouds are also holding back. Amazon’s Bedrock, Microsoft’s Azure Foundry and Google’s Vertex AI still do not support these Chinese open-weight models. Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Mandeep Singh and William Tong made the point after their token-volume mix reached 68%, following the launches of K3 and GLM-5.2.
Today the weights land
Moonshot is due to publish K3’s weights for public download on Monday, Bloomberg reported. Anyone will be able to download, modify and host the model. Daily sales at the Beijing company have risen at least sixfold since K3 launched.
That date was always in the diary. When Moonshot unveiled K3 on 16 July, the weights were the missing proof, promised for 27 July. They arrive into a market that spent the intervening fortnight learning to shop around.
Sam Altman saw the mood shift coming. “This is the first year where AI spend has been a big topic,” the OpenAI chief executive told CNBC this month. “And all of a sudden, it’s a very big topic.”

primary_article.title: How AI is becoming part of the American family
primary_article.text: AI's impact on American life isn't just at work . It's also at home, where it's helping with dinner and bedtime, learning our routines, overhearing arguments and never clocking out. Why it matters: The AI debate has largely focused on jobs and productivity . But a quieter shift is unfolding at home , where AI is also evolving from an on-demand assistant into an always-on presence that remembers, anticipates and increasingly acts like a member of the family. "The barriers to entry for families — in terms of cost and technical knowledge — are next to nothing," Sarah Dooley , founder of AI-Empowered Mom and author of an upcoming book on the topic, told Axios. "With lower barriers and adoption moving at lightning speed, impact and risks for families are often high." State of play: Domestic AI is already entering family life in several forms. The New Yorker recently profiled an Ohio mother and her two teen daughters whose relationships with AI ranged from household logistics to emotional support. The mother confided in an increasingly conversational Alexa, one daughter regularly talked to ChatGPT, and the other briefly opened up to a mental health chatbot, Tomo. The Cut profiled Jesse Genet — a former startup CEO and a mom to a blended family of seven kids — whose expanding staff of AI agents shops for groceries, helps run her children's homeschooling schedule and handles legal and financial paperwork. Last week, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI's first hardware device will be a screen-free, mobile smart speaker built to be a "humanlike AI companion that lives in the home." Zoom out: This trend goes well beyond the smart speaker wave of a decade ago. Earlier systems were often reactive and needed a command. The next generation of domestic AI can remember conversations, infer household patterns and adapt to individual family members. By the numbers: 81% of parents have used AI to help with parenting tasks, a Lurie Children's Hospital survey published in May found. Pew Research has found 64% of U.S. teens use chatbots, mostly for research and schoolwork, followed by fun and entertainment. Between the lines: The home may become AI's most intimate and least governed environment. Workplaces and schools are only just beginning to set formal guardrails around the technology. The unit of impact is often the family, not the individual users," Daniel Zhang , chief of staff at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, told Axios. "If one person chooses to engage with AI, the presence of that device or the model affects everyone in the household." But the effects depend heavily on how and where the technology is used. "It's hard to make broad claims because there's so much that matters in the details for these kinds of things," Anne Maheux, a developmental psychologist at UNC Chapel Hill who studies adolescents and AI, told Axios. For children especially, access, privacy and physical space matter. An AI device used openly in the kitchen is different from a chatbot a child accesses "privately in their bedroom," and both are different from a school computer that stays at school, Maheux said. For teens, AI can remove some of the friction involved in learning to navigate other people, uncertainty and conflict. Adolescence is a "particularly sensitive period" for developing social-emotional skills, Maheux says. The stakes are different from an adult outsourcing a skill they already have. What to watch: Nobody — not researchers, lawmakers, CEOs, parents or influencers — fully understands what it means to let AI into the most private parts of our daily lives. As Dooley points out, even free or low-cost AI comes with a complicated price tag: "We are paying with our data, with our stories, with our privacy." The bottom line: The office may be where AI changes the economy, but the home is where it could change us.

rationale: The article is squarely about AI entering family life and raises privacy, child-safety, and governance concerns, but it is a broad trend synthesis rather than a major new legal, policy, or technical development.
